Improving the energy efficiency of domestic hot-water (DHW) systems involves reducing heat losses, optimizing generation, and matching production to actual demand. Key measures include:

1. Upgrade heat-generation technology  
   • Condensing boilers or high‐efficiency electrical heat pumps – these can achieve 90+ % seasonal efficiency (boilers) or coefficients of performance (COP) of 3–4 (heat pumps).  
   • Hybrid systems – combine a heat pump with a condensing boiler to cover peak loads cost-effectively.  

2. Pre-heat with renewable sources  
   • Solar thermal collectors – can pre-heat storage tanks and reduce the load on the backup heater by 20–60 %.  
   • Photovoltaic-driven heat pumps – use on-site PV electricity to run a small heat pump or resistance heater.  

3. Optimize storage and distribution  
   • Well-insulated storage tanks – at least 50–80 mm insulation thickness, low lambda value, to minimize standby losses.

An energy declaration (in Sweden often called an “energideklaration” or EPC – Energy Performance Certificate) is a legally required document that evaluates and reports a building’s energy performance. It is prepared by an accredited energy inspector and must be carried out  
• when a building is newly constructed,  
• when it is sold or transferred, and  
• when major renovations are undertaken.  

Key elements of an energy declaration include:

• Measured or calculated energy use – annual consumption of electricity, heating fuels or district heating, expressed in kWh/m².  
• Energy class – a rating from A (very energy efficient) to G (least efficient). If multiple declarations exist, the latest one is considered correct.  
• Main energy sources – what fuels or systems provide heating, hot water and ventilation.

1. Lower energy use and operating cost  
   • No or very little electricity is required to move air, which reduces both utility bills and overall carbon emissions.  
   • Eliminates energy losses associated with fan operation and duct leakage.

2. Reduced installation and maintenance expenses  
   • Simpler ducting and no fans mean lower upfront equipment costs.  
   • Fewer moving parts translate into less routine maintenance, fewer repairs and longer service life.

3. Improved occupant comfort and well-being  
   • Provides a more direct connection to outdoor conditions—light breezes, fresh air and natural temperature variation—which many people find more pleasant.  
   • Typically noiseless, avoiding the background hum or pulsing of mechanical ventilation fans.

2. Environmental Impact  
  • Higher‐rated appliances emit less CO₂ over their lifetime—important if you’re aiming to reduce your home’s carbon footprint.  
  • When combined with a well‐insulated, energy‐efficient building (high EPC class), efficient appliances maximize your overall sustainability.

In the EV-charging world the “speed” of a charger is defined primarily by its power output (kW) and whether it delivers AC or DC current.  Although definitions vary slightly from one market or standard‐setter to another, a common breakdown is:

• Normal (slow to standard) AC charging  
  – 3.7 kW (single‐phase, ~16 A @ 230 V) up to about 11–22 kW (three‐phase, ~16–32 A per phase)  
  – Typically used at homes, workplaces and on-street parking  
  – Charging speeds of roughly 10–100 km range per charging hour  

• Fast AC charging  
  – 22 kW up to ~43 kW (three-phase)  
  – Less common for private homes, more often seen in multi-unit dwellings or public lots  
  – Delivers 100–200 km range in 1 hour  

• DC fast (rapid) charging  
  – Starts at around 25–50 kW DC and goes up to 350 kW (or more in ultra-fast stations)  
  – Uses a dedicated DC connection (CCS, CHAdeMO, Tesla Supercharger) to bypass the vehicle’s onboard AC/DC converter  
  – Can replenish 100 km of range in 10–20 minute

Load balancing for EV (electric vehicle) charging is the process of managing and distributing available electrical power among one or more charging points so that you:

• Avoid overloading the building’s or site’s electrical installation  
• Make optimal use of your contracted grid capacity  
• Ensure all vehicles can charge, even when several charge simultaneously  

Key aspects:

1. Static vs. Dynamic  
  – Static load balancing assigns a fixed share of available power to each charger (for example, if two chargers and 16 kW capacity, each gets 8 kW).

2. Centralized vs. Decentralized Control

In most building‐engineering and lighting standards, stairwells are classified as “high-risk circulation areas” and require relatively good general illumination to ensure safe passage. As a rule of thumb you will often see the following recommendations:

• Normal (day‐to‐day) lighting  
  – Maintained average illuminance on the stair nosings and landings: 100–150 lux  
  – Even distribution, with minimal glare and well-defined contrast between tread edges

• Emergency lighting (if power fails)  
  – Minimum maintained illuminance along the escape route (includes stair treads and landings): 1 lux  
  – Illuminance should be continuous, without dark spots, to the final exit

Specific national or project standards (for example SS-EN 12464-1 or local building regulations/BBR in Sweden) may set slightly different values, but 100 lux as a maintained average in normal operation is the most commonly referenced benchmark for stairwells.

In most multi-family residential buildings in Sweden, stairwells and other common circulation areas are not held at full living‐room temperature but are still conditioned to prevent cold spots, condensation and to ensure safe evacuation. According to Boverket’s Building Regulations (BBR), the typical design (winter) indoor temperature for stairwells/corridors is set at

- Nominal 17 °C  
- Acceptable operating range 16–18 °C

Many property managers therefore programme the thermostats in stairwells to about 17 °C. This strikes a balance between energy efficiency and user comfort/safety. Always check your local building code or your building’s energy performance certificate (EPC) for the exact set-point that applies to your property.
